{
  "Question": "A team of engineers is implementing a distributed metadata store for a cloud object storage system, using vanilla (single-instance) Paxos as the consensus algorithm for replicating metadata updates across 5 replica nodes, where proposer, acceptor, and learner roles are co-located on each node. To reduce end-to-end latency for client write requests, an engineer proposes modifying the core Paxos workflow as follows: after a proposer receives valid Phase 1 (Prepare) promises from a majority of acceptors for a given proposal number n and Paxos instance, the proposer will immediately execute the proposed write operation locally and return a success acknowledgment to the client, before sending any Phase 2 (Accept) messages to the acceptor quorum. Given this modification to vanilla Paxos, which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the consistency guarantees of the modified implementation?",
  "Options": [
    "A) The modified implementation preserves linearizable consistency for all write operations, as a Phase 1 quorum guarantee ensures no conflicting proposal for the same Paxos instance can be successfully committed, making early client acknowledgment safe.",
    "B) The modified implementation will only violate consistency if two concurrent proposers initiate proposals for the same Paxos instance with identical proposal numbers; otherwise, linearizable consistency is maintained.",
    "C) The modified implementation violates linearizable consistency, as a proposer cannot guarantee its Phase 2 messages will be accepted by a quorum even after receiving Phase 1 promises, leading to potential acknowledged writes that are never durably committed across the cluster.",
    "D) The modified implementation would preserve linearizable consistency if the team switched to Multi-Paxos with a stable elected leader, as the leader’s exclusive right to initiate proposals eliminates conflicts that would make early acknowledgment unsafe."
  ],
  "CorrectAnswer": "C",
  "Explanation": "Option C is correct: Paxos Phase 1 only grants a proposer the right to submit a proposal for a given instance, but does not guarantee the proposal will be accepted by a quorum. A higher-numbered concurrent proposal (or a new leader elected after the first proposer’s Phase 1 but before Phase 2 transmission) can obtain promises from a majority of acceptors, causing the first proposer’s Phase 2 messages to be rejected. This leads to a scenario where a client receives a success acknowledgment for a write that is never durably committed, violating linearizability.\nOption A is incorrect: A Phase 1 quorum does not block higher-numbered competing proposals from being committed, so early acknowledgment is not safe.\nOption B is incorrect: Consistency violations can occur even with distinct proposal numbers, as a higher-numbered proposal can preempt a lower-numbered one after the latter completes Phase 1; no duplicate proposal numbers are required for this failure case.\nOption D is incorrect: Even a stable Multi-Paxos leader cannot guarantee its Phase 2 messages will be accepted if it crashes or loses leadership after completing Phase 1 but before processing Phase 2, so early client acknowledgment remains unsafe."
}
